title: What is a fractional CRO, and do B2B founders actually need one?
description: What a fractional CRO does, how it differs from a sales hire, the signs you need one (and don't), and how to choose one in Australia.
answer: A fractional CRO (Chief Revenue Officer) is a senior revenue leader who works in your business part time, owning your growth strategy and helping you execute it, without the cost of a full-time executive. Most B2B founders under $5M in revenue don't need a full-time CRO. Many do need someone senior in their corner once referrals stop being enough and there's no one in the business whose job is growth.

sections.heading: What a fractional CRO actually does
paragraphs: A Chief Revenue Officer owns everything that brings money into the business: how you get found, how you win work, how you onboard new clients, and how you keep and grow them. A fractional CRO does the same job, just not five days a week.

The good ones don't hand you a strategy deck and walk away. They get in the trenches: building the target list, sitting in on pitches, setting up the pipeline and holding you accountable to the plan. The fractional part is about time, not commitment.

sections.heading: Fractional CRO, fractional growth leader or a sales hire?
paragraphs: Fractional CRO and fractional growth leader describe the same role. CRO is the familiar title if you've come from corporate or a scaled business. Growth leader is a more honest description for a small services firm: someone who drives growth across the whole business, not just sales.

A salesperson or business development manager is a different role. They run a sales process. A fractional CRO designs the process, builds the system and helps you lead it. Hiring a BDM before that exists usually means paying a salary for someone to work out what to do, and many salespeople don't understand how professional services actually wins work: through trust and relationships, not volume.

sections.heading: Signs you need one
paragraphs: You've grown on referrals and hit a ceiling, and growth has stalled even though the work is as good as ever.
Everything to do with winning new work still runs through you, and it slips every time you're busy delivering.
You're weighing up a sales hire or an agency, but you're not sure what you'd actually ask them to do.
You're ready for the next phase of growth, but there's no one in the business whose job is growth.

sections.heading: And when you probably don't
paragraphs: If you're booked out for the next year and have no interest in growing, you don't need one. Enjoy it.
If you already have a strong commercial leader in the business, you may need more capacity under them, not another leader above them.

sections.heading: What it costs and how much time it takes
paragraphs: A full-time CRO is a significant salary commitment that most businesses under $5M in revenue can't justify yet. A fractional arrangement scales that down to what the business needs right now, and flexes up as you grow.

The cadence varies. Some founders want a monthly strategy and accountability session. Others want embedded support that works more like a part-time team member. Be wary of anyone offering a fixed package before they understand your business.

sections.heading: How to choose a fractional CRO in Australia
paragraphs: You'll find fractional CROs in Australia through marketplaces that match businesses with fractional executives, through independent operators and through specialist firms. Whichever route you take, ask four questions. Have they carried a revenue number in a business like yours? Do they understand how professional services wins work? Will they build a system you keep, or one that leaves when they do? And will they work alongside you, or just advise?

At Tailwind Growth, that's the role Baidy Barton plays for founder-led B2B services businesses doing $200K to $5M in revenue: a fractional CRO and growth leader with 15+ years as a Commercialisation Director, Investor, Chief Revenue Officer of a B2B software company and Partner at a global professional services firm, paired with an AI-native growth system that handles the admin of winning new work.

faqs.q: How much does a fractional CRO cost?
faqs.a: It depends on how much time you need, but it's a fraction of a full-time executive salary. Tailwind Growth costs around 10% of a full-time Chief Revenue Officer, with no recruitment risk or employment overhead.

faqs.q: Is a fractional CRO only for tech startups?
faqs.a: No. Most fractional CROs come from scaling startups, but the role works just as well for B2B professional services firms such as lawyers, accountants, engineers and consultants, as long as the person understands how relationship-led businesses win work.

faqs.q: How long do you need a fractional CRO for?
faqs.a: Until the system runs and you, or a future hire, can lead it with confidence. Tailwind Growth works month to month with no lock-in.

title: Why B2B founders hit a referral ceiling — and how to break through it
description: Most B2B service businesses grow on referrals for a year or two, then plateau. Why it happens, the signs you've hit it, and the system that gets you through.
answer: Most B2B service businesses grow on referrals for the first year or two, then plateau. Not because the work got worse, but because referrals are random: you can't control who thinks of you, or when. Breaking through means adding a repeatable system: who you're targeting, how you'll reach them, and what happens to every opportunity once it exists.

sections.heading: The year-two plateau
paragraphs: Most SME founders grow through referrals in year one (and year two if they're lucky). Then growth hits a plateau. And it's confusing, because you're still doing great work. You look at peers whose businesses are starting to take off and wonder what they're doing differently.
Here's what it usually comes down to: they stopped relying on word of mouth and started using a proper system to manage their pipeline.

sections.heading: It's a system problem, not a quality problem
paragraphs: The ceiling isn't a sign your business is bad. Your clients love you. That's why the referrals came in the first place. The problem is that when winning new work depends entirely on who happens to think of you at the right moment, growth is out of your hands. You're not running a pipeline. You're waiting for luck.

The founders who beat the year-two blues don't necessarily have a better product or more talent (often the contrary). They have a process. They stick to it. And they're honest enough to bring in the right people to fill the gaps.

sections.heading: Signs you've hit the referral ceiling
paragraphs: Referrals have started to slow, and growth has stalled even though the work is as good as ever.
It's feast and famine: you're slammed with projects, then realise there's nothing lined up next.
Growing feels like "feeding the beast", and the only plan you have is to hustle harder.
Everything still runs through you, and new work only shows up when you personally make it happen.

sections.heading: What got you here won't get you there
paragraphs: If your growth has stalled, the question isn't "where have all the referrals gone?" It's "what system do I have for when they don't come?"

That system has three parts. Who you're targeting: the specific clients you want more of, not "anyone who needs us". How you're reaching them: the coffees, the events, the partners and the outreach, done consistently rather than when you have a spare minute. And what happens to every opportunity once it exists: a pipeline you actually manage, so nothing goes cold because you were busy delivering.

It also means reframing what "the work" is. Being the best in your business at delivering will only take you so far. After that, it's about your ability to build relationships with the people who'll matter to your business later. Organising the coffee, going to the after-hours event, getting out in market: that's the work.

sections.heading: The fix isn't another hire or another agency
paragraphs: Hiring a salesperson is expensive, slow to ramp, and they often don't understand how professional services wins work. A marketing agency is great at impressions but rarely focused on actual client acquisition. And more networking events on their own won't fix a missing system.
Referrals are an excellent starting point. Keep them. Just stop relying on them as your only source of new work.

faqs.q: Why do referrals stop working after a year or two?
faqs.a: They don't stop working, they just stop being enough. Your first referrals come from your existing network, and that network is finite. Without a system for reaching new people, growth plateaus once those first circles have heard of you.

faqs.q: How do I know if I've hit a referral ceiling?
faqs.a: Common signs are stalled growth despite great work, feast-and-famine cycles where busy periods are followed by an empty pipeline, and a sense that the only way to grow is to work harder personally.

faqs.q: Do I need to hire a salesperson to get past it?
faqs.a: Usually not in the early stages. A repeatable system for targeting, outreach and pipeline management, plus learning to lead sales yourself, typically gets B2B founders further than an early sales hire.

title: How do you grow a professional services business without hiring?
description: Before you add headcount, fix where your time goes. How founders win more work without a sales hire: automate the admin, lead sales yourself, and run a system.
answer: Fix where your time goes before you add headcount. Around 70% of the time founders spend winning work is admin: proposals, follow-ups and chasing. Automating that, learning to lead sales yourself, and running a repeatable pipeline system will usually grow a professional services business further than an early sales hire. If you need senior support, a fractional growth leader costs a fraction of a full-time hire.

sections.heading: Most of the time you spend winning work isn't selling
paragraphs: 70% of the time you spend winning work is admin. Not relationships or closing opportunities... admin. Proposals. Follow-ups. Chasing. Negotiating terms. Repeat.

I spent my career building high-growth businesses and I never had time. Of the 10 (1,000?!) tasks on my list that day, I was lucky to get through three. When you're that busy, it's easy for sales to fall down the list and become a future problem. I'd 'scale' into the weekend because so much of my time was taken up by the admin side of winning new work.
That's not a way to scale. It's a surefire way to burn out. And it's why the first instinct, to hire someone, often doesn't solve the actual problem.

sections.heading: Why your first sales hire probably won't save you time
paragraphs: First-time founders with deep subject matter expertise often ask me whether they should hire a sales rep or a BDM. They're not comfortable selling, or they haven't done it before. My advice probably sounds wrong coming from a growth professional: learn how to win work yourself. Founder-led sales wins out every time.

You won't save time by bringing someone on in the early days. Bringing them up to speed will eat your time. Teaching them the subject matter will eat your time. They'll expect all the collateral and material to enable them to sell, and you'll build that too. And they'll still drag you into every close, because at this stage the client is really buying you, the founder.

sections.heading: Winning work is coachable, not innate
paragraphs: Instead of hiring, invest in yourself. Learn how to articulate how you help. Take clients on a journey. Learn the process. Being good at winning new work is a skill you can build, not a personality trait you either have or don't.

The other half is prioritisation. When founders say they're "too busy" for the relationships that matter, it's sometimes delegation, but more often it's that everything feels urgent, so the important-but-not-urgent stuff loses. I learnt this the hard way at 23, when I was so deep in delivery for a major client that I never got the meeting with their incoming C-suite. When the retainer went out to tender, I had to hustle twice as hard.

sections.heading: What to put in place instead of a hire
paragraphs: Automate the admin. Use tools and AI for the proposals, follow-ups, research and pipeline tracking, so your time goes into the 30% that actually needs you: the relationship, the expertise and the judgement.
Run a repeatable pipeline system. Know who you're targeting, how you're reaching them, and what happens to every opportunity once it exists, so new work doesn't depend on referrals turning up.
Protect time for relationships. Put the coffees, events and check-ins in the calendar like client work, because they are client work.

sections.heading: Where a fractional growth leader fits
paragraphs: If you want senior help without a full-time hire, that's the gap a fractional growth leader fills: strategy, accountability and hands-on pipeline support, on a part-time basis. At Tailwind Growth, that's paired with an AI-powered growth system that handles the admin, for around 20% of the cost of a business development manager.

faqs.q: Should I hire a BDM or salesperson for my professional services firm?
faqs.a: In the early stages, usually not. Clients are buying the founder, so a new hire will still pull you into every close, and onboarding them eats the time you were trying to save. Learning to lead sales yourself and automating the admin is typically a better first step.

faqs.q: How much of a founder's sales time is admin?
faqs.a: In my experience, around 70% of the time spent winning work goes on admin such as proposals, follow-ups, chasing and negotiating terms, rather than on relationships or closing.

faqs.a: A senior revenue professional who works with your business part-time or embedded, giving you the expertise of a Chief Revenue Officer or Head of Sales without the full-time cost or commitment.

title: What are the alternatives to a marketing agency for B2B client acquisition?
description: Marketing builds visibility, but B2B services firms win clients closer to the sale. The alternatives that actually fill a pipeline, and when marketing makes sense.
answer: For most B2B services firms, the better alternatives sit closer to the sale: advocates and past-client referrals, partnerships, direct outreach, being in the room at industry events, and a pipeline system that follows every opportunity up. Marketing is great at amplifying those engines once they're running. It rarely replaces them.

sections.heading: Why marketing alone rarely fills a B2B pipeline
paragraphs: I know a business owner who spent money on a marketing campaign that produced plenty of traffic, but no leads. It helped with visibility, but none of it converted, and SMEs can't afford awareness that doesn't turn into meetings.
What actually moved the needle? Partners including her in RFPs unprompted. Past clients personally referring her to new businesses.

sections.heading: 1. Advocates and past clients
paragraphs: Your happiest clients are your best acquisition channel. Make it easy for them to refer you, stay in touch after the work ends, and invest in the customer experience while you're delivering. In B2B, the experience is the marketing.

sections.heading: 2. Partnerships
paragraphs: Firms that serve the same clients as you, but don't compete with you, can bring you into opportunities you'd never see otherwise. A handful of good partners who think of you first is worth more than a lot of impressions.

sections.heading: 3. Direct outreach, reframed
paragraphs: Most weeks I reach out to people I don't know to grab a coffee. I reckon 85% say yes. For years I didn't recognise that as cold outreach, because I'd reframed it as reaching out to someone I admire, am interested in, or can learn from. Before that reframe, I was terrified of rejection.
It totally is cold outreach, though, and it's one of the most underrated growth levers there is. Most people avoid it because it gives them the ick. All you have to do is reframe it.

sections.heading: 4. Being in the room
paragraphs: Organising the coffee, attending the after-hours event, getting out in market, connecting in real life at the conference: that's the work. Being the best at delivering will only take your business so far. After that, it's your ability to build relationships with the people who'll matter to your business later.

sections.heading: 5. A system that follows everything up
paragraphs: None of these channels work if opportunities go cold because you were busy delivering. A simple, repeatable pipeline, with clear next steps for every conversation, is what turns activity into clients.

sections.heading: When a marketing agency does make sense
paragraphs: Marketing absolutely has a place. But B2B businesses should get their inbound and outbound engines running and nail the customer experience first, because advocates and partnerships offer a higher return in the early days. Get that humming, then turn to marketing to amplify it.

faqs.q: Is a marketing agency worth it for a small B2B services firm?
faqs.a: Often not as a first step. Agencies are strong at visibility, but small B2B firms usually win clients through relationships, referrals and partnerships. Get those working first, then use marketing to amplify them.

faqs.q: What's the cheapest way to get B2B clients?
faqs.a: Past-client referrals, partnerships and direct outreach to people you'd genuinely like to meet cost mostly time, and convert far better than paid awareness for most professional services firms.

faqs.a: No. Tailwind Growth focuses entirely on client acquisition and pipeline, not brand awareness or ad campaigns. It combines a fractional growth leader with an AI-powered growth system, for around a third of the cost of a traditional agency.

title: What does "AI-native" actually mean for a B2B services business?
description: Everyone's calling themselves AI-native. What it really means for a services business, why the margin hype misses the point, and why people still come first.
answer: An AI-native services business is designed around AI from the ground up. AI handles the research, admin, follow-up and pipeline tracking behind the scenes, so people spend their time on the client relationship, expertise and judgement. It isn't adding ChatGPT to an old workflow, and it isn't replacing the people clients are actually buying.

sections.heading: AI-native isn't the same as using AI
paragraphs: Every agency and consultant is calling themselves AI-native right now. Most of them mean they've added ChatGPT to their workflow. That's not the same thing.

AI-native means the way you deliver is designed around AI from the start, not retrofitted. In a growth system, that means AI handles the research, the personalisation, the follow-up sequencing and the pipeline tracking that used to need either a full sales team or hours of the founder's time.

sections.heading: The margin hype misses the point
paragraphs: There's a lot of talk about AI-native services as a new utopia: use AI to automate the work traditionally done by grads, keep charging the same, and enjoy 60–80% better margins.

I agree there's a huge opportunity. But a lot of the people saying this have never operated a services company. Most fail to recognise that an unbeatable customer experience is where the true value and differentiation lie. No one's going to keep buying if you leverage the heck out of AI and deliver a rubbish outcome.

On margins, I expect downward price pressure, as clients expect you to be more efficient in your delivery. Ultimately I think we'll see a more fragmented market, with more phenomenal boutique players that start eating Big Four consulting's lunch.

sections.heading: Good AI should be invisible
paragraphs: Good AI use shouldn't be in your client's face. It should be seamless and behind the scenes: automation, background research, enabling processes.
Don't use it for your differentiation, which is usually your voice and your point of view. That's the part clients are paying for.

sections.heading: What AI-native looks like at Tailwind Growth
paragraphs: When I was brainstorming Tailwind in the car on the way to the beach, my thesis was that it had to be "people first, AI-native". The "people first" part has been proven true every single day since.

In practice, AI handles the 70% of winning work that was always admin. You handle the 30% that needs you: the relationship, the expertise, the judgement. A solo founder with the right system can run a pipeline that used to need three or four people. Not because AI replaces the human connection, but because it handles everything that isn't human connection.

faqs.a: A business or service designed around AI from the ground up, rather than one that has added AI tools to an existing workflow.

faqs.q: Will AI replace professional services firms?
faqs.a: Unlikely. AI will take over much of the admin and junior work, but clients still buy expertise, judgement and relationships. Expect more efficient boutique firms and price pressure on routine work.

faqs.q: What is an AI-native B2B growth partner?
faqs.a: A growth partner whose system uses AI for prospecting research, follow-up and pipeline management, combined with a senior person who handles strategy and relationships. Tailwind Growth is one example, built for Australian B2B services founders.

title: Why pipeline concentration is a growth risk (and what to do about it)
description: When a few clients make up most of your revenue, one phone call can upend your business. Why feast or famine isn't bad luck, and how to reduce the risk.
answer: When a small number of clients make up most of your revenue, one phone call can wipe out your capacity plan and your cashflow. Feast or famine usually isn't bad luck. It comes from focusing 100% on delivery. You reduce the risk by keeping pipeline work going during busy periods, and by regularly stress-testing your model with one question: what happens if we lost this client?

sections.heading: Five buckets of hummus
paragraphs: I eat a lot of hummus. My daughter eats a lot of hummus. Heck, hummus is a whole family staple. I also hate going to Woolies more than once a week.

One week we had five buckets of hummus in the fridge (too many, or a new record, depending on how you look at it). But I'd rather have five buckets than one. Because that last bucket will definitely be borderline empty when I reach for it on Tuesday night. Cue a meltdown.
Your client base works the same way.

sections.heading: What concentration risk looks like in practice
paragraphs: I work with a founder who had two key clients, both on an embedded partnership model. In the same month, one client called to cut their hours by 66%, and the other cut back by 55%.
Suddenly they were scrambling, chasing new leads to fill their team's spare capacity, and managing cashflow to cover payroll.

sections.heading: Feast or famine isn't bad luck
paragraphs: It's the result of 100% focus on delivery, and not stepping back to ask "what happens if we lost this client?", even when things are going well.

It's an easy trap. When a big client is keeping you busy, pipeline work feels optional. I've been there: early in my career I was so deep in delivery for a major client that I never built the relationships with their new leadership. When the work went out to tender, I had to hustle twice as hard.

sections.heading: How to reduce pipeline concentration risk
paragraphs: Keep the pipeline moving when you're busy. Busy periods are exactly when pipeline work gets dropped, and exactly when you need it most, because the next opportunity takes months to land.

Stress-test your model. Step back regularly to poke and prod your business: which clients would hurt most to lose, how quickly could you replace them, and what's your cashflow runway if they cut back?
Build relationships beyond your main contact. Know the decision-makers, especially when leadership changes.
The goal is that when a client calls to halve their spend, it's an inconvenience, not DEFCON 1.

faqs.a: The risk that comes from relying on a small number of clients for most of your revenue, so losing or downsizing one of them has an outsized impact on capacity and cashflow.

faqs.q: How do I stop the feast-or-famine cycle?
faqs.a: Keep doing pipeline work during busy periods, track opportunities in a simple system, and regularly ask what would happen if your biggest client left.

faqs.q: How many clients is too few?
faqs.a: There's no fixed number, but if losing any single client would force you to cut staff or scramble for cashflow, your revenue is too concentrated.
